system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: NMOSD is an autoimmune astrocytopathy strongly associated with IgG antibodies against aquaporin-4, a water channel enriched on astrocytic endfeet in the optic nerves, spinal cord, and area postrema. Attacks commonly manifest as optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and area postrema syndrome.
vignette: A 34-year-old woman develops painful loss of vision in the right eye. Six months later, she has rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention. Spinal MRI shows a T2-hyperintense lesion extending from C4 through T2. During the week before the weakness began, she had persistent hiccups and vomiting without gastrointestinal disease. Brain MRI does not show the typical periventricular lesions of multiple sclerosis.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Multiple sclerosis can cause optic neuritis and myelitis, but a longitudinally extensive cord lesion plus area postrema symptoms is substantially more characteristic of NMOSD.

MOG antibody-associated disease can produce optic neuritis and myelitis and is a legitimate close differential, but the combination of longitudinally extensive myelitis and classic area postrema syndrome most strongly supports NMOSD; AQP4 testing would be the next discriminating test.

Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is typically a monophasic, often postinfectious syndrome with encephalopathy and multifocal CNS lesions, unlike these separated optic-spinal attacks without encephalopathy.
Spinal cord infarction can cause abrupt myelopathy but does not explain a prior optic neuritis attack and area postrema syndrome.
key_expl: NMOSD classically affects the optic nerves and spinal cord and may involve the area postrema, causing otherwise unexplained hiccups, nausea, or vomiting. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and recurrent optic neuritis are high-yield clues. The disorder is strongly associated with AQP4-IgG and is distinct from multiple sclerosis.
objective: Recognize NMOSD from the optic-spinal-area-postrema pattern, especially longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.
clues: cord lesion spanning multiple vertebral segments
absence of classic MS MRI pattern
